summary: For ages 5–7, this is a star-pattern recognition and sky-orientation topic. Children learn that people have picked out patterns among the stars and given them names (constellations and smaller star patterns), starting with the Big Dipper / the Plough. Strictly, the Plough is part of a bigger constellation called the Great Bear, and it is easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere. They practise re-finding that seven-star saucepan shape in a busy star field, use the two 'pointer' stars at the end of the bowl to find the North Star (Polaris), and come to understand that a constellation is a named pattern people imagined, not a group of stars joined together. Keep it recognition-and-naming, not astrophysics.
misconceptions: The stars in a constellation are close together / physically joined in space (they only appear as a pattern from Earth; they can be hugely different distances away)
The constellation lines are really drawn/visible in the sky (the lines are imaginary aids; people invented the patterns and names)
The North Star is the brightest star in the sky (it is not especially bright; it is useful because it sits above the north pole)
Constellations are fixed pictures that look obviously like their names (they are loose patterns that take imagination to see)
The star patterns are in exactly the same place all night / all year (they appear to move; deeper seasonal change is a later topic)

activities.title: Connect the dots to find the Plough, then find it again
steps: Look at a night-sky scene scattered with stars and join seven of them, dot-to-dot, into the saucepan shape of the Big Dipper / the Plough
Say or hear the name once the shape is built
Then look at a busier star field and point out (or re-join) the same Plough shape hidden among many more stars, proving you can re-find it yourself
If possible, go outside on a clear night or use a planetarium/star app and try to spot the real Plough in the sky
activities.insight: A constellation is a pattern you can learn to recognise and re-find; the Big Dipper is the easiest first pattern to pick out.

activities.title: Use the pointer stars to find north
steps: Starting from the built Plough, draw or trace a line from the bottom pointer star through the top pointer star (the two stars at the end of the bowl furthest from the handle), and keep going out past the top of the bowl
Follow that line to a lone star and name it the North Star (Polaris)
Say what the pattern is useful for: it helps you find which way is north
activities.insight: The two end-of-the-bowl stars 'point' to the North Star, so the pattern has a real job — it helps you find north. For people in the Northern Hemisphere, Polaris is useful because it marks north and barely moves, not because it is the brightest star.

activities.title: Are the stars really joined up there?
steps: Guess whether the seven Plough stars are really joined together or close to each other in space
Reveal the answer (for example by lifting a flap, tapping, or being told the explanation)
Talk about how different cultures looked at the same stars and imagined different pictures and names
activities.insight: The connecting lines are imaginary — people joined the dots and named the picture. The stars are actually enormous distances apart and only line up into a shape when seen from Earth; from another viewpoint the pattern would fall apart.

activities.title: Quick check: match, name and point
steps: Pick which pattern is the Big Dipper from a few options
Match the pattern to its name
Show or say which way the pointer stars point (trace a path or choose an answer)
activities.insight: Recognising the Plough and recalling the pointer-to-North-Star fact are things you can now do.

checkQuestion: The seven stars of the Big Dipper (the Plough) make a shape like a saucepan. Are those stars really close together and joined up in space — or do they just LOOK like a pattern from where we stand on Earth? Tell me which, and WHY.
checkAnswer: They just look like a pattern from where we stand. The stars are not joined and are actually enormous distances apart — some far behind others — but from our viewpoint on Earth they happen to line up into a shape that people long ago named. A constellation is a pattern of stars that people have named, not a bunch of stars stuck together.
